headings.title: Introduction to Acquired Immune Deficiencies
headings.content: Unlike primary immune deficiencies which stem from inherited genetic mutations present at birth, acquired immune deficiencies develop later in life due to external environmental factors, infections, medical treatments, or systemic illnesses. These conditions progressively damage a previously normal immune system, leaving the individual vulnerable to opportunistic infections and malignancies that a healthy immune system easily repels. In clinical practice across Nigeria, secondary immune deficiencies frequently complicate prevalent infectious diseases like severe malaria or measles, alongside widespread nutritional challenges. Understanding this distinction helps differentiate congenital anomalies from acquired vulnerabilities during patient assessment.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Mechanisms of Immune System Decline
headings.content: The structural decline of an acquired immune deficiency typically targets key orchestrators of the immune response, most notably CD4+ helper T-lymphocytes. When pathogens or destructive processes deplete these regulatory cells, the entire cellular and humoral defense network collapses. Cytokine production falters, B-cells lose necessary activation signals, and cytotoxic T-cells fail to recognize infected host cells. This systemic breakdown explains why individuals experience multiple, concurrent infections involving unusual or opportunistic organisms that rarely trouble immunocompetent persons.

headings.title: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) and Progression to AIDS
headings.content:
Human Immunodeficiency Virus infection remains the most prominent model of acquired immune deficiency worldwide. The virus uses its surface glycoprotein gp120 to bind specifically to CD4 receptors on target cells, fusing its viral envelope and releasing single-stranded RNA into the host cytoplasm. Through reverse transcriptase, the viral RNA is converted into DNA, integrating permanently into the host genome. 

- **Acute Infection**: High viral replication occurs alongside a temporary drop in CD4 counts, often accompanied by flu-like symptoms.
- **Clinical Latency**: The virus replicates at lower levels while the immune system fights back, a phase that can last years without treatment.
- **AIDS Stage**: CD4 counts drop below 200 cells per microliter, giving rise to severe opportunistic infections and defining malignancies.

headings.title: Secondary Immunodeficiencies Caused by Malnutrition and Infections
headings.content: While viral pathogens take center stage, nutritional deficiencies represent a massive driver of acquired immune impairment globally. Severe protein-energy malnutrition causes thymic atrophy, reduces lymphocyte counts, and impairs secretory antibody production at mucosal surfaces. Additionally, acute and chronic systemic infections such as measles, malaria, and severe tuberculosis temporarily or persistently blunt immune responsiveness. In resource-constrained environments, the dangerous synergy between chronic hunger and recurring infections creates a compounding cycle of immune failure.

headings.title: Iatrogenic Causes of Acquired Immune Deficiency
headings.content: Medical interventions designed to treat other pathological states can inadvertently induce acquired immune deficiencies. These iatrogenic causes include immunosuppressive drug regimens utilized following organ transplantation, chemotherapy agents that target rapidly dividing bone marrow progenitor cells, and long-term systemic corticosteroid therapy. While these treatments are lifesaving for managing autoimmune disorders or malignancies, nurses must remain vigilant in monitoring patients for signs of secondary infection due to drug-induced leukopenia and suppressed inflammatory cascades.

headings.title: Clinical Assessment and Diagnostic Evaluation
headings.content: Detecting acquired immune deficiencies requires a combination of thorough clinical history-taking and targeted laboratory investigations. Nurses should look out for red flags such as recurrent, severe, or unusual infections, persistent oral thrush, chronic unexplained diarrhea, and significant weight loss. Diagnostic evaluation relies heavily on complete blood counts with differential to identify leukopenia or lymphopenia, alongside specific assays like CD4 T-cell enumeration and viral load testing for HIV. Early identification prevents catastrophic systemic complications.

headings.title: Nursing Management and Patient Care Strategies
headings.content: Holistic nursing care for patients with acquired immune deficiencies centers on infection prevention, nutritional support, and medication adherence. Strict adherence to standard precautions and rigorous hand hygiene protects vulnerable patients from hospital-acquired pathogens. Nurses must also educate patients on safe food preparation, avoiding raw or undercooked foods, and recognizing early signs of infection to seek prompt medical intervention. For individuals on complex antiretroviral regimens, adherence counseling is vital to prevent viral resistance and treatment failure.

headings.title: Prevention, Treatment, and Public Health Considerations in Nigeria
headings.content: Public health strategies addressing acquired immune deficiencies in Nigeria require a multi-faceted approach combining community education, routine screening, and accessible treatment services. Prevention programs focus on preventing mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT), promoting safe sexual practices, and improving nutritional security in vulnerable communities. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is widely available through government and partner-supported clinics, transforming a fatal diagnosis into a manageable chronic condition. Community health nurses play a pivotal role in dispelling stigma, encouraging testing, and supporting long-term retention in care.
